title: ‘House of the Dragon’ Actor Benjamin Evan Ainsworth on ‘Absurdity’ of Assassination Attempt, Daeron’s Growing Power and if Ormund Is Dyeing the Kid’s Hair
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for Season 3, Episode 3 of “House of the Dragon,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	Daeron Targaryen (Benjam
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for Season 3, Episode 3 of “House of the Dragon,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	Daeron Targaryen (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) is growing up: On this week’s episode of “House of the Dragon” Season 3, the youngest (and least blonde) child of Alicent Hightower (Olivia Cooke) and Viserys Targaryen (Paddy Considine) experienced his very first assassination attempt!


	While sharing a meal with his cousin/keeper Ormund Hightower (James Norton) and his uncle Gwayne Hightower (Freddie Fox) in Tumbleton, a group of Baratheons tried to kill the young prince seemingly on the orders of his half-sister, Queen Rhaynera Targaryen (Emma D’Arcy). The attack was unsuccessful, as Gwayne jumped to his nephew’s rescue in time, which only resulted in a couple of deaths and Ormund projectile vomiting at the smell.
	

	But the latest deadly move between the “Blacks” (who currently hold the Iron Throne through Rhaynera) and the “Greens” (who are splintered off into multiple factions) will have a profound effect on Daeron heading into the final two episodes of “House of the Dragon” Season 3.



	

					Ormund Hightower (James Norton) in “House of the Dragon”
									Courtesy of HBO
	



	“I think shock is a big part of that scene in general,” Ainsworth tells Variety. “This is an escalation he wouldn’t have ever expected. There’s also this idea of the power dynamics between him and Ormund leveling out and clashing in a way. ‘Bold’ Jon Roxton there has very much been a man who’s followed Ormund’s orders, and it’s the first time I’m trying to stop him, and Ormund’s ordering him to do something. So there’s something about that which is stepping up this dynamic within this group amidst the chaos of everything.”
	

	Daeron holds back Ser Jon Roxton (Joplin Sibtain) when he attempts to dive into the situation and stop Gwayne, before Ormund realizes Gwayne has sussed out the assassination plan before it’s begun. And that little bit of leadership from Daeron, combined with his disgust with Ormund’s handling of the situation, could fuel how Daeron continues to respond to Ormund’s attempts to make him the new king.



	

					Gwayne Hightower (Freddie Fox) in “House of the Dragon”
									Theo Whiteman/HBO
	



	“He’s trying to take more ownership of the situation, but also that’s over the bedrock of just shock and tension and a frustration, too, with Ormund and the way that he’s almost debilitated by his senses,” Ainsworth says. “And he’s throwing up right next to me. And there’s an absurdity to that scene, which Daeron is feeling just in the shock of it in itself. Let alone the dead bodies everywhere.”

	It’s Gwayne’s arrival in Tumbleton after he’s left Fabien Frankel’s Ser Criston Cole (RIP) that has Daeron really thinking through what role he needs to play in this ongoing war.



	

					Criston Cole (Fabien Frankel) in “House of the Dragon”
									Theo Whiteman
	



	“It’s exactly that. The verb ‘thrust’ feels correct because it’s almost a violent thing,” Ainsworth says. “He’s suddenly within the chaos, and so I don’t think he’s had much time to think about it or to process it, which is why there’s so much tension inside of him and in this desperation he has with Gwayne. In the scene he has with Gwayne, he’s almost forced to think of the idea of becoming king, just what would that mean? Would that mean space between him and Ormund?”

	After weeks of buildup, it’s clear after this week’s assassination attempt that “House of the Dragon” Season 3 is about to feature a confrontation between the Blacks and the Greens in Tumbleton. Would Daeron, who takes to fencing in the courtyard after his brush with death, be capable of joining the fight if it comes to that? After all, he is known as “Daeron the Daring” in George R.R. Martin’s “House of the Dragon” source material, “Fire & Blood.”

	“I think he would be. Whether he’s ready, I think that’s something he’s questioning himself,” Ainsworth says. “It’s the reason he goes out to spar after that assassination scene. There’s an element of getting away from the stresses of things and focusing on something that he enjoys, something that he’s good at. But he’s also proving to himself that he can protect himself if something like that happens again. And he knows Ormund and Gwayne are watching him, too. So I don’t want to spoil anything either way.”
	

	Read more from Variety’s interview with Ainsworth below.
	
		How do you view Daeron’s relationship with his uncle Gwayne in comparison to what we’ve seen between him and Ormund? Gwayne is the first other member of the family we’ve seen Daeron interact with since we met the character.	

	There’s a growing tension and growing stakes within Tumbleton this season. And this episode feels like the power dynamics are really pushing and grating against each other within Ormund and Daeron’s relationship. And Gwayne is a figure in his life who is more of a brotherly uncle, someone he can speak with, can connect with, and doesn’t have to cover himself up or conceal anything in any way with. It’s very much a breath of fresh air and needed; confiding away from Ormund’s chaos and manipulation.

	I think this version of Daeron was always the center, and then when it’s with Ormund, I felt it was just more so covering up and containing, and he was thinking more about every choice, everything he says. Whereas with Gwayne, it’s much more instinctual. There’s a safety he feels with Gwayne that just isn’t there because of how dangerous Ormund can be and this kind of twisted feeling of needing Ormund’s affection, as well. Being the perfect squire, being the perfect version of Daeron around him, and there’s a part of that which has made him a more balanced person. He’s been away from the sour politics of King’s Landing, his brothers, his half-sister. It’s all kind of crazy, and he’s managed to live away from that. But I think this season poses a completely different prospect because he’s thrust in the middle of the chaos.



	

					Rhaynera Targaryen (Emma D’Arcy) in “House of the Dragon”
	


	
		Have you seen the fan theories that Ormund not only dyed the fake Daeron’s hair blonde, but that he’s actually been dyeing the real Daeron’s hair a Hightower color for years because Ormund hates the Targaryens?	

	I have seen that. Do you know what, it’s funny because it wouldn’t be too far-fetched for Ormund to think of something like that. He seriously is the type of guy to do that. It’s been so cool to see all of the audience reception and theories and the excitement that people have for the character in the show is beyond me.

	There’s an element to it where it wasn’t explicitly said when we were on set either way. So there’s a world in which that could be happening, but I don’t know. I think there’s something quite nice about him having his mother’s hair, there’s this connection he feels. He hasn’t seen his mother in years, but he’s made an ideal image of what his mother might be in the hope of some kind of other future for him. So the hair being the same, and the green colors, and the picking of his nails, things like that — I think it’s quite nice to draw that link between Alicent and Daeron.
	
	
		We’ve only seen Daeron with his dragon Tessarion once because Ormund keeps the dragon locked away. Do you think his relationship with his dragon is different from his siblings who don’t have to keep their dragons locked up?	

	I think he has a really good relationship with Tessarion. She’s been his constant throughout his time in Old Town, a friend who’s always been there for him. Gwayne comes and goes. As we see in this season, he’s returning after a long time away. But Tessarion’s always there and there’s a love and a deep appreciation that goes both ways with them. And it’s something that I think keeps him hopeful about his Targaryen side, because we’ve seen the rhetoric that Ormund has against the Targaryens. He thinks that their blood is tainted and it’s an obscenity to have dragons. Yet [Daemon’s] relationship with Tessarion is what I think is keeping him balanced and not just a pawn for Ormund’s use.



	

					Alicent Hightower (Olivia Cooke) in “House of the Dragon”
									Ollie Upton
	


	
		I know all the cast members decide their own ways they want to approach the character based strictly on the scripts or also George R.R. Martin’s books. Are you a “Fire & Blood” reader or not?	

	I’ve read from Aegon’s conquest to [the plot of] Season 3, because I wanted to know what has happened, because he’s grown up in Old Town under the Faith of the Seven. I feel like he would have a base understanding of those concepts and I wanted to be able to bring that into the character. And he would have learned about the history. But I also quite like giving room for this character to grow. 

	I’m aware of “Daeron the Daring” and where this character goes, and the reputations he has within the books. But I think it’s quite cool to try and explore those reputations within the show and within the scripts as well, these morally gray characters and the interpersonal relationships so brilliantly written and well acted by James Norton and Freddie Fox and to get to share that with them has been awesome.
	
		This smell thing is a real problem for Ormund. Do you think Daeron has used that at all to his advantage throughout his childhood?	

	Oh, I think it’s definitely something he’s been aware of throughout his childhood, but I don’t think he’d then do anything about it or manipulate. I think, if anything, his involvement with Ormund’s senses would be to try and help. I imagined him putting together pomanders for him, because it’s those things to please him in order to almost save his own ass, as well.
	
	
		There’s a scene in this episode that cuts off after Daeron asks Gwayne if he saw his mother, Alicent, when he was last in King’s Landing. Was there more to this scene? Did Gwayne have an answer for him?	

	I don’t know exactly what was said, but I remember talking with Freddie and there is a moment at the end of that scene, which I don’t think made the cut, but where he comes to me, he puts his arm around my shoulder and then we go off. That’s the screenplay version, at least anyway. I think there’s something about, even if he is going back to Old Town, there’s still a sensitivity there. And they have a deep respect for each other. I think their dynamic is one to look out for, and one that means a lot to Daeron.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘House of the Dragon’ Actor Benjamin Evan Ainsworth on ‘Absurdity’ of Assassination Attempt, Daeron’s Growing Power and if Ormund Is Dyeing the Kid’s Hair

title: Kevin Feige Says Ryan Coogler Met With David Jonsson Six Months Ago in a ‘Secret Meeting’ to Discuss ‘Black Panther 3’ Role: ‘I Got Chills’
description: Marvel boss Kevin Feige recently told Empire how David Jonsson was cast as the next Black Panther. He explained that “The Long Walk” star met with “
body:
Marvel boss Kevin Feige recently told Empire how David Jonsson was cast as the next Black Panther. He explained that “The Long Walk” star met with “Black Panther” director Ryan Coogler in a “secret meeting,” and that the Oscar winner quickly identified Jonsson as his next leading man.

	“We hadn’t started a search yet,” Feige explained. “Ryan was working on ‘Sinners,’ and when Ryan works on a project he’s all in. So the presumption very much was we would sit with him after ‘Sinners’ came out, after the Academy campaign. We were waiting ’til after the Academy Awards to sit with Ryan and begin that process.”
	

	He added, “A month and a half or so before that process, he called me and said, ‘I found him’. I said, ‘What do you mean?’ He goes, ‘I found him. He’s this guy, David Jonsson.’ He mentioned his movies. I had seen some of them. I watched more. He goes, ‘I’m going to meet him.’ He had a secret meeting with him under cloak of darkness in a hotel somewhere, and called me afterwards and said, ‘He’s the guy, he’s the guy, I felt it. I felt it in my soul. He’s a good man, and he is the next Black Panther.’ And I got chills, and I got a little welled-up and said, ‘Let’s do it’. So we’ve been sitting on this secret for a good five or six months.”


	Jonsson will play T’Challa’s son in “Black Panther 3,” which hits theaters Dec. 15, 2028. The announcement was made during Marvel’s Hall H panel on Saturday at San Diego Comic-Con. Original cast members Leticia Wright and Winston Duke are returning for the new chapter, which follows Prince T’Challa II as he comes of age and takes up the Black Panther mantle.
	

	After Chadwick Boseman died of colon cancer at age 43 in 2020, Wright was the first to take over as the Black Panther in 2022’s “Wakanda Forever.”

	Marvel launched the first “Black Panther” in 2018 to overwhelming acclaim. It grossed $1.3 billion at the worldwide box office and earned seven Oscar nominations, including best picture.

schema.headline: Kevin Feige Says Ryan Coogler Met With David Jonsson Six Months Ago in a ‘Secret Meeting’ to Discuss ‘Black Panther 3’ Role: ‘I Got Chills’

title: Tom Holland: Some of My Movies Are ‘S–t’ and You ‘Shouldn’t’ Watch Them
description: Tom Holland is having a great time doing the press circuit for both “The Odyssey” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” because he’s fond of the movies. T
body:
Tom Holland is having a great time doing the press circuit for both “The Odyssey” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” because he’s fond of the movies. That hasn’t always been the case.

	On the July 22 episode of Dish Podcast, Holland spoke with hosts Nick Grimshaw and Angela Hartnett about the press cycles surrounding films — and how he’s had to occasionally talk up a project that he’s not particularly fond of.


	“I’m absolutely loving it. When you’re doing press for movies you’re really proud of, it’s really easy,” he said. “Because when they ask you questions about why should people go and watch this movie, you’re not lying to anyone. You really feel like people should go see it. I’ve had experiences before when people say, ‘Why should you see this movie?’ And in the back of your mind, you’re like, ‘You shouldn’t, because it’s shit.’”
	

	The quality of the films has turned the process around for the actor, especially in a summer where he has two blockbusters coming out.

	“It’s felt really like a bit of a victory lap, to be honest,” Holland said. “I’ve really enjoyed it. I’m super proud of both of the films.”

	Also in the interview, Holland reveals that he’s learned more about the art of doing press from his “Odyssey” co-star, Anne Hathaway.

	“I’ve had the pleasure of sitting down with Anne Hathaway for the last three days and doing press with her,” he said. “For me, that’s been an awesome learning experience. She’s such a pro.”

	Watch the full podcast episode below.

schema.headline: Tom Holland: Some of My Movies Are ‘S–t’ and You ‘Shouldn’t’ Watch Them

title: Gracie Abrams Scores First No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘Daughter From Hell’
description: Gracie Abrams has earned her first No 1 on the Billboard 200 with her third album “Daughter From Hell,” bowing atop the chart with 124,000 equivalen
body:
Gracie Abrams has earned her first No 1 on the Billboard 200 with her third album “Daughter From Hell,” bowing atop the chart with 124,000 equivalent album units.

	The singer-songwriter announced the album back in May, along with the release of its first single “Hit the Wall.” Her last project, 2024’s “The Secret of Us,” became her first to hit No. 1 in the United Kingdom, Australia and the Netherlands. The album peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and led into a world tour that year and a subsequent arena run in 2025.
	

	Abrams recently announced the 64-date “Look at My Life” international arena tour, which will set sail across North America in December and continue through March 2027 before moving onto Europe next April and May. The North American leg will include 37 shows and kicks off at Denver’s Ball Arena before wrapping up March 16-20 with a four-night stint at Brooklyn’s Barclays Center. She will then take a three-week break before resuming in the U.K. and Europe for 27 shows, including four nights at London’s O2.


	Elsewhere on the albums chart, Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” lands at No. 2, followed by Morgan Wallen’s “I’m the Problem,” Ella Langley’s “Dandelion” and Noah Kahan’s “The Great Divide.” Drake’s “Iceman” comes in at No. 6, while Future’s “The Real Me” dips from No. 1 to 7. Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” ticks up from No. 9 to 8, while Morgan Wallen’s “One Thing at a Time” holds at No. 10.

	BTS, meanwhile, makes the most noise in the top 10 this week as “Arirang” rebounds from No. 26 to 9. The album, which debuted at No. 1 following its release in March, got a surge thanks to the release of a vinyl picture disc edition.

schema.headline: Gracie Abrams Scores First No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘Daughter From Hell’

title: Gay Romance Podcast ‘Drive Thru Magic’ Casts Daniel J. Kim and Danielle Kennedy, Sets September Release Date (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Daniel J. Kim (“Cobra Kai”) and Danielle Kennedy (“The ’Burbs”) have joined the cast of “Drive Thru Magic,” the upcoming scripted fiction podcast fr
body:
Daniel J. Kim (“Cobra Kai”) and Danielle Kennedy (“The ’Burbs”) have joined the cast of “Drive Thru Magic,” the upcoming scripted fiction podcast from actor, writer and director Briggon Snow (“The Bright Sessions”).

	The project is produced by Atypical Artists and executive produced by Lauren Shippen.

	“Drive Thru Magic” is a gay romance drama set against the unlikely backdrop of a roadside drive-thru, where two men find each other in the small, repeated moments between a menu speaker box and a car.
	

	The first episodes will drop Sept. 7 on all podcast platforms.


	Kim will voice Louie, a pre-med student passing time in a drive-thru job, who falls for a repeat customer. Snow will also star as Gabe, a young man caring for his grandmother as she loses herself to dementia, who finds an unexpected anchor in the voice on the other side of the speaker. Kennedy will play Barb, a biting, no-nonsense drive-thru lifer and the closest thing Louie has to a friend.

	“I’m so thrilled to have Daniel and Danielle helping me tell this story,” Snow said in a statement. “I started working on this back in 2024 and kept walking away because it was at times a little too close. It’s rooted in something I’m still living through, but pushing through and creating this show has sort of been my way of facing hard loss and change. I wove it into a gay love story because grief needs somewhere to live, and love felt like the right place.”

	Atypical Artists is behind such audio fiction hits as “Two Thousand and Late,” a dark comedy about our modern world and a 2026 Tribeca Audio Showcase selection, “The Bright Sessions,” a science fiction drama about people with supernatural abilities in therapy, “In Strange Woods,” the acclaimed original musical following a young girl after the loss of her brother as she tries to learn to survive, and Netflix’s “Stranger Things” spinoff “Rebel Robin: Surviving Hawkins.”
	

	“Like everything Briggon makes, ‘Drive Thru Magic’ is so heartfelt, funny, and swoon-worthy,” Shippen said. “His writing perfectly intertwines love and grief — you’ll immediately fall for these characters and wish you could spend even more time with them. There are few writers and actors out there who can make you feel as deeply as Briggon and Atypical Artists is so honored to be stewarding this story.”

	The series wrapped recording in Los Angeles earlier this summer.

	Snow is represented by Eileen O’Farrell Personal Management and Dean Panaro Talent (voice). Kim is represented by Management 101 and Osbrink Talent Agency for voice. Kennedy is represented by Eileen O’Farrell Personal Management and Avalon Artists Group.

schema.headline: Gay Romance Podcast ‘Drive Thru Magic’ Casts Daniel J. Kim and Danielle Kennedy, Sets September Release Date (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Soars to $639 Million Globally After Two Weekends, Including $140 Million in Imax
description:
Christopher Nolan‘s star-studded adaptation of “The Odyssey” has surpassed $600 million globally after just two weekends of release.

	The big-budge
body:
Christopher Nolan‘s star-studded adaptation of “The Odyssey” has surpassed $600 million globally after just two weekends of release.

	The big-budget take on Homer’s 3,000-year-old epic, led by Matt Damon as the Greek king Odysseus, has generated $639.6 million worldwide, including $353.2 million at the international box office and $284.4 million domestically. It’s a staggering turnout for a sword-and-sandal adventure that’s nearly three hours long and rated R, underscoring the fact that Nolan is the most bankable director of his generation.
	

	Over the weekend, “The Odyssey” generated $128.3 million from 81 overseas markets, a remarkable 10% decline in holdover territories. It’s the best second weekend hold for a movie that opened above $100 million, according to Universal, which backed the $250 million-budgeted film. “The Odyssey” has already surpassed the international haul of this spring’s hit “Project Hail Mary” ($340 million) and now ranks among the top five highest-grossing Hollywood releases of the year — and that’s before opening in major foreign markets including China, Japan and Korea. Top-earning territories to date include the United Kingdom and Ireland with $46.3 million, France with $31.8 million, Italy with $28.8 million, Australia with $20.6 million and Germany with $20.4 million.


	Imax has contributed an incredible $140 million of global ticket sales for “The Odyssey,” which is notable as the first feature shot entirely with Imax cameras. It’s the second-fastest title in the company’s history to surpass $100 million, following 2019’s behemoth “Avengers: Endgame,” with Nolan’s epic taking just 10 days to hit the mark.
	

	In its second weekend of release, “The Odyssey” amassed $24 million internationally and $38 million worldwide in Imax, ranking as the company’s largest sophomore outing in history. Imax’s coveted 70mm screens — Nolan’s preferred format — accounted for $5.2 million over the weekend from just 41 screens across the world. The small-but-mighty 70mm footprint has generated $16.9 million to date, representing 12.1% of the total Imax box office. Since there are so few of those screens across the globe, most of those showtimes are sold out into September.

	“Chris has crafted the type of masterwork that draws our biggest fans back to experience it two or three times — while introducing entirely new fans to Imax,” says Imax’s CEO Richard Gelfond. “We are only beginning to see the impact that will have on our brand and business.”

	In other global box office milestones, Disney and Pixar’s “Toy Story 5″ has surpassed $1 billion and stands as the highest-grossing movie of 2026 with $1.02 billion. It’s the third release of the year, following “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” ($1.001 billion) and “Michael” ($1.001 billion), to cross the coveted box office benchmark. “The Odyssey,” as well as next weekend’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” are basically assured to join that elusive company.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Soars to $639 Million Globally After Two Weekends, Including $140 Million in Imax

title: ‘Attack on Paradise’ Review: Under Siege From Both Criminals and Cops, a Hero Battles Upward in a Zesty High-Rise Actioner
description: Saïd Boumazoughe gets a “created by” credit just below director Bob Colaers at the end of “Attack on Paradise,” amplifying the fact that this projec
body:
Saïd Boumazoughe gets a “created by” credit just below director Bob Colaers at the end of “Attack on Paradise,” amplifying the fact that this project is very much the Belgian-Moroccan star’s realized personal fantasy of an action vehicle. That translates into something a lot like “Die Hard,” with elements of “Assault on Precinct 13,” “High Rise” and more thrown in — albeit with a distinctly more diverse cast/character roll call, reflecting both the actor’s own background and Antwerp’s multicultural modern reality.
	

	That adjustment aside, there’s nothing conceptually very original to this tale of a prodigal son returning to find his cranky old ma requiring rescue from both organized crime and a police raid. But it’s got energy and style to spare, making for a genre exercise whose pleasures considerably outweigh its familiarity. If Belgian action cinema is probably not going to be the next big thing, nonetheless this highly enjoyable, good-humored effort should help it make some headway abroad.


	Lanky, hoody-clad Suleyman (Boumazoughe) is minding his own business walking home one night when a car nearly runs into him, triggering some choice words. Unfortunately the unmarked vehicle’s drivers are cops all too willing to arrest and pin dubious charges on their non-white, gangbanger-looking quarry. Seven years later, our hero gets released from prison. He heads straight to infirm mother Fatma (Fatima Khanfour), who turns on a dime from tears of joy at this return to slap-happy rage over his “abandonment.”

	But all too soon, there are far worse perils to worry about. In his absence, the housing project Suley grew up in got taken over by the crime boss known as Prince (Achmed Akkabi). That international fugitive from justice has turned its seventeen stories into his personal underworld HQ. Police have until now treated this illicit empire as a “no-go zone.” Today, however, they’re finally executing a long-planned raid to seize the boss, shut down his operations, and put everybody in prison—though apparently racking up casualties is expected, even encouraged.
	

	Alas, the bad guys are very well prepared for just such an occasion, in terms of surveillance cameras as well as heavy artillery. Worse yet for our protagonist, this battle kicks off just moments after his maternal reunion, when he’s gone to the building’s basement to retrieve belongings in storage. The mayhem is so immediately widespread, simply getting back up to mom’s flat proves life-threatening.

	Suleyman gains a reluctant ally in cop Yasmine (Clara Claymans), as the rest of her SWAT team gets swiftly exterminated. He commits to helping her cause, too — which means fighting off Prince’s innumerable flunkies and his chief lieutenants. The latter consist of brutish pro boxer The Lion (Jamal Ben Saddik), former Congolese child soldier Minza (Rudy Mukendi), Albanian gun runner Tchuko (Soroush Helali), and drug-deals overseer Nikita (Imanuelle Grives), who is extra-problematic because she and Suleyman used to be an item.

	The headlong pacing allows nary a breather, though there are enough wry notes, character quirks and offbeat details (remote-control doors, goats, a knife fight on a waterbed) to prevent macho monotony from setting in. With scant time for backstory, we must simply accept that Suley is a near-invincible one-man army, and Boumazoughe’s air of beleaguered resourcefulness makes that easy to swallow. The supporting figures are colorful enough, though Akkabi’s sneering chief villain arguably makes less of an impression than his subordinates.

	“Colorful” is definitely the word for Steven Vanvolsem’s cinematography, which bathes the gritty settings in candied hues — another credulity-stretching element that works just fine. Editor Brian Ent helps punch across physical action that is not dazzling à la “John Wick,” going instead for an entertainingly messy, not-too-acrobatic tenor. As energy continually ramps upward, the score by Maxim Lany and Jonas Nuttin moves from ominous horns to pulsing electronica, with some neat incorporation of prayer-call-like motifs underlining the hero’s Muslim faith.

	If the script by Sven Huybrechts (of WWII thriller “Torpedo”), Boumazoughe and fellow cast member Salahdine Ibnou Kacemi is the most routine element here, it nonetheless rehashes well-worn ideas at a brisk clip. The climax could be a little more climactic, but otherwise Colaers’ second directorial feature — following smaller-scaled horror comedy “Trizombie” — provides too good a time while you’re watching to quibble about how quickly it may fade from memory.

schema.headline: ‘Attack on Paradise’ Review: Under Siege From Both Criminals and Cops, a Hero Battles Upward in a Zesty High-Rise Actioner

title: ‘Am I Supposed to be a Comedian?’: Donald Trump’s Bizarre White House Correspondent’s Dinner Speech Had Few Laughing
description: Even by the standards to which we’ve all, by now, become accustomed, President Donald Trump’s performance at Friday night’s White House Corresponden
body:
Even by the standards to which we’ve all, by now, become accustomed, President Donald Trump’s performance at Friday night’s White House Correspondents’ Dinner was bizarre. And the fact of it — from the style of his halting delivery to the substance of his vindictive message to a journalists’ group who’d handed him a mic — made clear that he’s now in something of a spiral. A public figure who, more than any politician or celebrity in our history, has placed the desire for approval at the center of his brand is being confronted by his dwindling popularity. (His approval rating was one of the topics Trump touched upon in a speech that felt less like what he calls “the weave” than like a ramble.) He doesn’t like that his style is falling out of favor, and he’s going to make sure, for the next two-plus years or perhaps even longer, that we know he doesn’t.
	

	Trump’s speech Friday night served as a re-do of the planned address he was meant to give at the original 2026 WHCD in April, which was marred by a gunman firing shots inside the Washington Hilton. He had promised, then, to excoriate the press; on a rescheduled and more somber evening months later, he seemed unsure, at first, how to act. “Let’s have a little bit of fun,” he said. “What do we do here? Is this supposed to be fun, am I supposed to be serious, am I supposed to be a comedian?” But old reflexes kicked in: Just before this, Trump had complained about the evening’s awards, which had gone to various journalists whose work (naturally, given their profession covering the current administration) had been adversarial to his interests. “This has not been an easy evening, all those awards,” he said. “Do I have a say?” Later, he’d go on to criticize journalists including CNN’s Kaitlan Collins and the Wall Street Journal’s Josh Dawsey by name. 
	

	It’s an article of faith among the online #Resistance that Trump’s never having won an Emmy for “The Apprentice” is a crucial part of his origin story; just because an insight has been dulled by repetition, though, doesn’t make it untrue. The White House Correspondents’ Dinner is an evening of entertainment programming and an awards ceremony. The latter thing seems to activate something primal within Trump; the former presents for him an opportunity to redefine reality along his own terms, and to force an increasingly bored and quiet audience along for the ride. (Indeed, during his speech, Trump recollected the 2011 Correspondents’ Dinner, at which then-President Barack Obama brutally roasted him, as a fun evening he enjoyed, especially because it felt good to be at the center of attention. That is not how the event is widely remembered!)

	There was an air of flop sweat to the evening: Like any inept emcee, Trump began blaming unnamed joke writers for basic material — light, sub-Friars Club material lovingly roasting his allies Nicki Minaj and Bari Weiss — falling flat, but his own delivery seemed oddly nervous. In the past, Trump has dominated journalists. Indeed, he’d told the world that’s what he planned to do at April’s first version of this event. Instead, though, Trump seemed affronted and almost frightened of the crowd before him when discussing his own popularity, and diminished as he ran through tired material: The Oscars’ decline in ratings over time, for instance, or his antipathy to Chris Christie, Bruce Springsteen and Jane Fonda. 

	Once, Trump’s raging against the Oscars had a certain charge to it. That’s not because his claims that the show’s ratings are down because of how liberal celebrities are (there’s a lot more to it than that), but because, as a seeming vanguard of seismic cultural change, Trump had the power to subsume basically any entity. Now, though, it’s just sadly predictable. This man has been the defining element of American politics for ten years. We know that he cares a lot about awards! We don’t need to be told again!

	That, more than sorrow over the American President going after journalists or mild bemusement that he couldn’t land a Borscht belt joke about an aging Senator unable to consummate his marriage any longer, feels like the takeaway from a vexed, pointless hour of speech. The strange and at-times unknowable mind that even recently gave us turns of phrase like “the late, great Hannibal Lecter” is now hung up on a public that, faced with inflation and an unpopular war in Iran, isn’t laughing anymore. And that mind’s response is to return to safe and comfortable territory, re-fighting old battles with Rosie O’Donnell and with various awards-giving bodies. The show has lost even what lurid appeal it might have held for Trump’s morbidly curious critics. And yet it will go on, and on. Trump vowed, jokingly-but-not, to run for re-election (which the Constitution bars) in 2028. And yet listening to his deflated delivery, one could tell that his heart wasn’t in it. Perhaps he was thinking about who’d won the awards earlier that night.

schema.headline: ‘Am I Supposed to be a Comedian?’: Donald Trump’s Bizarre White House Correspondent’s Dinner Speech Had Few Laughing

title: ‘No Rest for the Wicked’ Review: A Supernatural Gay Love Story in a 19th-Century Backwater
description: The yearning separations of seafaring life have generated many a romantic ghost story, and while it largely takes place on terra firma, the Danish “
body:
The yearning separations of seafaring life have generated many a romantic ghost story, and while it largely takes place on terra firma, the Danish “No Rest for the Wicked” provides an honorable addition to that roster. Kaspar Kalle’s assured debut feature, drawn from an 1884 story by German author Karl Heinrich Ulrichs — a very early proponent for gay rights — walks a sometimes murky line between love story and horror. But the more sinister aspects ultimately turn out to be deliberate misdirection in this tale of two men who find each other in the remote Faroe Islands of the mid-19th century. In the end, any uneven qualities in Kaspar Kalle’s handsomely atmospheric sophomore feature dissipate in a melancholy poignancy reminiscent of “Brokeback Mountain” and “All of Us Strangers.”
	

	In 1862, Baldur (Egor Venned) is a taciturn young man living with widowed mother Asla (Sofia Nolsoe). Going out one day to fish alone, he’s engulfed by mysterious clouds, then hears cries for help — though once he accidentally hits his head on a rock, it’s Baldur who’s rescued by Helge (Pilou Asbaek), a 40-ish sailor who’d become lost on an unfamiliar side of the island. They make it back to Asla’s cabin, where she’s charmed by their gregarious guest. Baldur is more circumspect, irked at having temporarily lost his boat in the mishap, and unsettled by Helge’s teasing manner, which could be interpreted as either adversarial or flirtatious. Nonetheless, the visitor fills his head with thoughts of adventure, and the many things Baldur has never seen — neither a tree or a mountain, for starters.
	

	Later, their tentative friendship turns into something more passionate — to the dismay of eavesdropping Asla, who realizes she is not the party Helge’s charm was aimed at. When a whaling ship docks, both men are now ready to sign on as crew. But having already sacrificed a husband to the sea, Baldur’s mom balks at losing her only child as well. Maternal guilt works its magic, leaving Helge to sail off alone. Ill winds, however, force his return all too soon — as one of many corpses washed ashore from a shipwreck. Aggrieved, Baldur makes a blood wish that his lover “come back.”

	At this point, things take a supernatural leap that has already been portended by various visions and nightmares. Is Helge some “force of evil,” as Asla suggests, even a vampire? When she grows alarmed enough to alert other villagers to her fears, the sailor’s dug-up corpse proves disconcertingly warm and  undecayed, and a contagion of sorts begins spreading to others.

	Ulrichs’ brief original tale reads more like a plot outline than fully-realized fiction, almost as if it were intended for oral recitation. The screenplay by Rasmus Birch and Kalle makes useful changes on that template, replacing crudely literal-minded aspects with more suggestive ones, paring dialogue to make room for effective visual storytelling. They get an excellent assist in that department from cinematographer Jacob Moller, who makes the most of poetically stark locations. That imagery is complemented by persuasive period design elements, and an original score by Hettarher that encompasses some wordless choral passages.

	A successful model (and Faroes native) making his screen debut, Venned sports the kind of looks and physique that are almost too idealized for the setting. They further make him an odd partner for conspicuously older Asbaek, who’s in ingratiating form. But the newcomer holds his own acting-wise with his much more experienced costar. Nolsoe provides strong support. In her role as well as elsewhere, Kalle downplays the explicit homophobia that might have rendered this a more simplistic allegory, making Asla less a figure of interfering jealousy than a woman who simply doesn’t want to be abandoned yet again. Love finally triumphs in “No Rest for the Wicked,” a denouement that both is haunting, and requires a literal haunting to arrive.

schema.headline: ‘No Rest for the Wicked’ Review: A Supernatural Gay Love Story in a 19th-Century Backwater

title: ‘Pinocchio: Unstrung’ Review: Killer Puppetry Is the Best Thing About This Killer Puppet Slasher
description: British indie director Rhys Frake-Waterfield gained a measure of notoriety for his 2023 film “Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey,” at best an amusing
body:
British indie director Rhys Frake-Waterfield gained a measure of notoriety for his 2023 film “Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey,” at best an amusing sketch idea that could hardly support a feature-length horror movie, let alone a very slapdash sequel. But it wasn’t memorably bad enough to merit either cultists or a shelf full of Razzies, both of which it found: As a prankster on a shoestring budget, Frake-Waterfield has technical resourcefulness and even a bit of wit. Both are again in evidence on his latest, “Pinocchio: Unstrung,” though so are are clear shortfalls in storytelling and basic scare-mongering. Anyone who was tickled by an evil Pooh Bear may get a kick out of an evil Pinocchio, but the director’s so-called Twisted Childhood Universe remains a pretty old-hat idea, not mined here with any great daring.
	

	Conceptually, a Pinocchio horror film is less of a lark than a Winnie-the-Pooh one, in large part because “Pinocchio,” in its original pre-Disney form, was already plenty macabre as a story. Though it too strayed pretty far from Carlo Collodi’s 19th-century novel, Guillermo del Toro’s Oscar-winning 2022 stop-motion version reclaimed some of that dark spirit with a Fascist Italy milieu, baroque flashes of violence and the vividly personified presence of Death throughout. It did not, however, feature the eponymous wooden marionette gleefully peeling the skin off people’s faces, so “Pinocchio: Unstrung” has its own USP.


	What it does have in common with del Toro’s film is the craggy, splintery, roughly handmade design of Pinocchio himself, a far cry from the smoothly rounded cartoon child of many childhood imaginations — and something of a triumph for the film’s puppetry and animatronic departments, on whom the film is pleasingly reliant. (They’re also proudly showcased in behind-the-scenes footage that runs through the closing credits.) The gore effects here are, for the most part, similarly organic and old-school: “Pinocchio: Unstrung” is never especially frightening, and even its jump scares are oddly muffled, but it is abundantly gross and grisly in all the ways a cheap-and-cheerful slasher should be. 
	

	There’s more visual initiative on display here than there was in “Blood and Honey,” though it starts, like that film, with a simply animated prologue. Styled to evoke shadow theater, it lays out the thin backstory of how Geppetto — a wealthy British inventor in this contemporary telling, more mad scientist than humble carpenter, and played by “Game of Thrones” alum Richard Brake — came to craft the timber tyke in a deliberate effort to create artificial life. When his grandson James (Cameron Bell) is orphaned following a car accident, he takes on another surrogate son, but keeps the two boys separate in his spooky Gothic mansion, until Pinocchio’s restless, rule-breaking curiosity gets the better of him.

	Though James is initially freaked out by this talking log, it isn’t long before the two bond as brothers, and James — against Geppetto’s firm orders that Pinocchio never leave the house — smuggles his new friend to school in his backpack. There, Pinocchio witnesses James being bullied by his peers, and his vengeful instincts kick in. (He also witnesses James’ dental appointment after school, and similarly sees red: Suffice it to say the puppet’s sense of right and wrong needs some tweaking.) From here, the film lurches from one brutally bloody setpiece to the next, most of them rather sketchily set up by Frake-Waterfield’s semi-coherent script, as Pinocchio also harvests the human organs that he believes will make him one of them. (The fact that Geppetto gave him no manhood has not escaped his notice.) The most inventive kill here — set in a school gym, cuing death by treadmill and falling weights — is also the least motivated, but no matter.

	Sharper, nastier jokes would make up for the more slipshod writing here, as would a bit more high-camp vim in the performances, though it’s fun hearing Robert Englund pop up as a particularly cursed (and nameless) incarnation of Jiminy Cricket. Meanwhile, the film’s scrappy, tactile visual rewards are sometimes let down by a muddy sound mix. “Pinocchio: Unstrung” is an exercise in swings and roundabouts, then, but it also shows Frake-Waterfield settling into a style and ethos as a filmmaker: His provocations may be goofy, but here they feel more spirited, and less calculated for viral impact, than in his previous work. As B-horror auteurs go, he may yet be a real boy.

title: Berlin Pride Terror Suspect Dead After Confrontation With Police
description:
Berlin Pride Terror Attack
                          Suspect Killed by Police
body:
Berlin Pride Terror Attack
                          Suspect Killed by Police
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The suspect accused of plowing a van into a crowd near Berlin's Pride festival and attacking others with a machete is dead after a confrontation with police, authorities say.
      
    
            German officials say Abdul Ballout was killed Sunday following a nearly 24-hour manhunt ... after Saturday's attack left one person dead and 29 others injured.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Berlin prosecutors say Ballout previously sought to join the Islamic State group, and authorities are investigating the Pride attack as an act of Islamic extremist terrorism.
      

            Berlin Police released a statement on X ... claiming Abdul is said to have rushed toward emergency forces with a stabbing weapon, after which police firearms were used. Despite immediate resuscitation measures initiated by the Berlin Fire Department, he died at the scene.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... cops say Ballout barreled into Tiergarten -- Berlin's most prominent park -- and plowed through people near the Pride parade route before fleeing the scene. Police said some victims suffered life-threatening injuries, while others had stab wounds.
      
    
            The bloodshed unfolded just a few hundred yards from a party that was supposed to close out Berlin's annual Pride festival ... prompting officials to cancel the remaining celebrations.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hundreds of thousands of people had attended Berlin's Pride parade, which is one of Europe's largest LGBTQ+ celebrations.
      
    
            A crowd reportedly gathered at a memorial near the crime scene Sunday to mourn the victim and show support for Berlin’s LGBTQ+ community. German officials have vowed to strengthen security at future public events.

description:

                          Club Waves Knick In, Checks the Net
body:
NYC Basketball Stars
                          Club Waves Knick In, Checks the Net
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Club security had two very different questions for New York’s NBA stars Saturday night ... "Michael who?" and "Right this way, Mr. Brunson."
      
    
            Video posted Saturday night shows Brooklyn Nets star Michael Porter Jr. towering over the crowd outside the club as security appears to check whether his name is on the list.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Then Jalen Brunson's ride pulls up ... and the Knicks captain and reigning NBA Finals MVP steps out and heads straight inside without breaking stride.
      

            In other words ... Net, you on the list? Knick, go right in!
      
    
            Alix Earle arrives moments later and makes her way inside, too ... while MPJ’s brief guest-list screening makes the New York basketball hierarchy look pretty official.
      
    
            Brunson did just lead the Knicks to their first NBA title in 53 years ... so these days, his face might be the only reservation he needs.

title: TikTok Star Rebecca Luna Dies at 49 with Medical Aid, After Sharing Alzheimer’s Battle
description:
TikTok Star Rebecca Luna
                          Dies at 49 with Medical Aid, After Alzheimer's
body:
TikTok Star Rebecca Luna
                          Dies at 49 with Medical Aid, After Alzheimer's Battle
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                July 26, 2026
                
                            8:49 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  July 26, 2026
                                10:42 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Rebecca Luna, the TikTok creator who openly documented her fight with young-onset Alzheimer’s disease, has died at 49 after choosing to die via medically assisted suicide.
      
    
            Luna’s death was announced Saturday, July 25, in a post shared on her TikTok account ... saying she passed away at approximately 1:15 p.m. surrounded by loved ones.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The British Columbia, single mom gained a following after revealing her Alzheimer’s diagnosis in April 2025 at age 48. She spent the months that followed sharing raw updates about her condition, doctor visits, and her decision to pursue MAID.
      

            Luna also became an advocate for end-of-life choices, using her platform to answer questions and provide resources for others facing similar decisions.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Her story caught the attention of singer Lily Allen after Luna shared that meeting the pop star was on her bucket list. The two eventually met at one of Allen’s concerts, an experience Luna called "the best."
      
    
            Just days before her death, Luna told followers she had moved up her MAID date from early August to July 25, explaining that the decision was ultimately about taking control of her own life.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            In her final message, Luna reflected on her journey, saying she had learned to stand up for the younger version of herself and hoped others would learn to love themselves. "If I can do it, you can do it too," she told her followers.
      
    
            Luna leaves behind a community of fans who followed her story and praised her for bringing awareness to Alzheimer’s and end-of-life conversations.
      
    
            Rebecca Luna was 49.
      
    
            RIP

title: D4vd Apple Music Account Hacked, Fake Song Posted Amid Preliminary Hearing
description:
D4vd
                          Apple Music Profile Hacked, Fake 'I Did It' Track Posted
body:
D4vd
                          Apple Music Profile Hacked, Fake 'I Did It' Track Posted
                          While Singer Remains Behind Bars
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Amid singer D4vd being locked up and currently fighting to keep his murder case from going to trial, his Apple Music page has been hacked ... posting a fake song with a voice sounding like the jailed artist professing his love for the victim Celeste Rivas.
      
    
            The falsified track, titled "I DID IT" surfaced over the weekend, despite David Anthony Burke -- the artist known as D4vd -- remaining behind bars, without access to upload music himself. The track's artwork also features an aerial photo of D4vd's Tesla in the L.A. tow yard where Celeste's dismembered body was discovered last year.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The chorus repeatedly names Celeste ... describing her as "the girl with my name tattooed on her chest" and claiming her scent remains on his clothes "like cigarettes." The voice, mimicking D4vd's voice, also sings about hearing Celeste whenever he breathes ... missing her and fearing she will only love him after he dies.
      

            The timing couldn't be more jarring as Burke remains jailed without bail as his preliminary hearing unfolds in Los Angeles ... detailing the gruesome evidence prosecutors have against the singer.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ has reported ... prosecutors spent the past week laying out evidence they claim connects D4vd to Celeste's killing, including messages revealing tension between the pair shortly before her death. The court also heard D4vd had "Celeste" tattooed on one of his fingers, while prosecutors say Celeste had his name inked on hers.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            D4vd has pleaded not guilty to murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains. The preliminary hearing will continue this week.
      
    
            We've reached out to Apple Music and Burke's camp ... so far, no word back.
      
      
              
          
                          
                Celeste Rivas
              
                          
                D4vd
